title: Canker sores: caring for mouth ulcers and knowing when to seek help
intro: An aphthous ulcer, often called a canker sore, is a painful shallow sore in the lining of the mouth. It may make eating, brushing and talking uncomfortable even when it is small. Typical canker sores are not contagious and often heal without specific treatment. However, not every sore inside the mouth is an aphthous ulcer, so a persistent or unusual lesion needs examination rather than repeated self-treatment.

sections.heading: Recognising a familiar pattern
paragraphs: Typical sores may have a pale centre and a red edge and occur on the inner lips, cheeks or tongue. Some people have occasional episodes; others develop recurrent crops. Larger or numerous ulcers can be more troublesome and take longer to settle. Cold sores are a different condition and can sometimes occur inside the mouth too, so location alone cannot confirm the diagnosis. A dentist or clinician can assess a sore whose appearance or behaviour is unfamiliar.

sections.heading: Why an assessment may be useful
paragraphs: The cause of recurrent aphthous ulcers is often unclear. Family susceptibility, minor injury and stress may play a part. A sharp tooth, poorly fitting denture or accidentally biting the cheek can also cause a traumatic ulcer. Medicines, nutritional deficiencies and some digestive or inflammatory diseases can cause other forms of ulceration. Tell the clinician about new medicines, bowel symptoms, skin problems, joint symptoms or sores elsewhere. Blood tests are sometimes appropriate; recurrent ulcers do not automatically mean a deficiency.

sections.heading: Make eating and cleaning gentler
paragraphs: Try soft foods and cooler drinks, and temporarily avoid foods or drinks that sting, such as very spicy, acidic, rough or very hot items. Clean gently with a soft toothbrush instead of abandoning oral hygiene. A dentist can address a rubbing denture or sharp tooth; do not try to file the tooth yourself. Notice repeat irritants without excluding large groups of nutritious foods. A brief record of episodes, possible triggers and healing can make a later consultation more useful.

sections.heading: Treatment aims to ease the episode
paragraphs: A pharmacist or dentist may recommend a suitable pain-relieving preparation, mouthwash or local corticosteroid treatment. Choice depends on age, other illnesses, pregnancy and whether the sore is actually aphthous. Follow the product instructions and check suitability for children; do not share someone else's prescription. More severe recurrent disease may need specialist care. Available treatments can ease pain or shorten an episode, but do not reliably prevent every future recurrence. Taking high-dose vitamins without an established need is not a substitute for assessment.

sections.heading: When to seek medical or dental help
paragraphs: Have an ulcer checked if it lasts longer than three weeks, differs from your usual sores, bleeds or becomes increasingly red and painful. Seek advice earlier for very large or numerous ulcers, frequent disruptive episodes or symptoms elsewhere in the body. Persistent ulcers occasionally have a serious cause, including oral cancer; checking them is a precaution rather than a diagnosis. Get prompt help if pain prevents adequate drinking or you become generally unwell, especially with a weakened immune system. Difficulty breathing or severe difficulty swallowing needs emergency help.

examples.title: A rubbing denture — hypothetical example
examples.text: A sore repeatedly appears where a denture rubs. The person arranges a dental review rather than using numbing gel indefinitely. The dentist checks the lesion and the fit, and explains when to return if it does not heal.

examples.title: Repeated episodes with other symptoms — hypothetical example
examples.text: Someone has recurrent sores and ongoing bowel symptoms. They bring a medicine list and an episode record to their clinician. Any investigations or supplements are based on the assessment rather than assuming every ulcer is caused by a missing vitamin.

questions: Does this look like an aphthous ulcer, injury or another condition?
Which treatment is suitable for my age, health and other medicines?
What healing time and recurrence pattern should prompt another examination?
